11664-the-camp-fire-girls-do-their-bit-o:
Hildegard G. Frey's 1919 Camp Fire Girls book sends the Winnebagos over the top with the war effort. A long train stops at a mountain station, and Lieutenant Allison wakes with a start as the journey breaks.

Nyoda, the group's lodestar, oracle, and elder sister, draws the girls together, and no one girl has more say than the others. Agony, new to the group, finds harmony instead of a single guardian's sway. The book follows camp, work, and wartime service, with the Winnebagos learning to do their bit in a world at war.
12868-the-harp-of-god-proof-conclusive-t:
J. F. Rutherford's Harp of God, published in 1921 by the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, is a Bible study textbook for beginners. Its title promise, that millions now living will never die, frames chapters on creation, justice, the Abrahamic promise, the birth of Jesus, the ransom, resurrection, and restoration. Questions and Scripture citations run throughout.

The book teaches in numbered paragraphs, asking readers to prove each point from Scripture, from the nature of Adam's death to the value of Christ's ransom price. Its tone is confident and didactic, aimed at new students. The volume is a key document of early Jehovah's Witness teaching.
14412-the-history-of-the-great-irish-fam:
The Reverend John O'Rourke wrote this history of the Great Irish Famine of 1847, in a third edition of 1902. He dedicates it to his fellow countrymen, as a record of a terrible episode in Irish history. O'Rourke writes from Irish sources and eyewitness tales. He covers earlier famines too, and the blight that struck the potato. The book aims to set the leading facts down without delay.

O'Rourke faults the Labour-rate Act, which set the nation's bone and sinew to cutting hills and filling hollows on byways where no work was wanted. Roads rose where none were needed, and an inspector called them works that only blocked traffic. Later pages tell of typhus in workhouses, coffins on donkey carts, and families eating roots and asses' flesh. The book stands as a stern, sorrowful record of a nation's trial.
16565-history-of-the-expedition-under-th:
Paul Allen prepared this history of the Lewis and Clark expedition for the press, by order of the United States government, covering 1804 to 1806. A map of the track from the Mississippi to the Pacific fronts the volume. Chapter one sets out from Wood River, describes St. Charles, the Osage and Kanzas rivers, and the character of the Osage Indians, with their curious tradition of origin.

Later chapters follow the party up the Missouri, across the Rockies, and down the Columbia. The narrative is the founding account of the great western journey. Readers of exploration will find a detailed, official record of America opening to the Pacific.
23427-evolution-old-new-or-the-theories-:
Samuel Butler wrote this long study comparing older theories of evolution with that of Charles Darwin. Buffon, Erasmus Darwin, and Lamarck each get a full hearing, set against Darwin's account, with Paley's natural theology and a Nature review of Butler's own Life and Habit framing the debate.

Butler argues that want of field knowledge led some critics astray. He adds that knowing the use of an end and the fit of means to it can ground sound reasoning even where much stays unknown. The prose is learned, combative, and at times wry, aimed at readers who follow science and its quarrels. The book matters as a Victorian counter voice, defending earlier thinkers and pressing Darwin's followers to face the gaps in their own case.
27279-southern-literature-from-1579-1895:
Louise Manly wrote this large survey of Southern writing from 1579 to 1895, published in Richmond in 1900. She wrote it to give school children and general readers a way into American life and history through Southern authors. Long extracts sit beside criticism, so readers meet the writers in their own words before Manly judges them.

The book can serve as a reader beside a history text or as the base for close study of Southern life and letters. It closes with a full list of Southern authors. Its range runs from early colonial writing to the end of the nineteenth century. For anyone tracing how the South wrote about itself, it remains a useful one-volume map.
34101-a-bilateral-division-of-the-pariet:
Ales Hrdlicka wrote this anatomical paper, extracted from the Bulletin of the American Museum of Natural History, volume thirteen, article twenty-one, pages 281 to 295, dated New York, December 31, 1900. Hrdlicka treats a bilateral division of the parietal bone in a chimpanzee, with special reference to oblique sutures in the parietal.

The first such case in apes, described by Johannes Ranke in 1899, was an adolescent female orang among 245 orang skulls in the Selenka collection at Munich. Its abnormal suture split the right parietal into a larger upper and a smaller lower part. The paper serves students of ape anatomy and human variation.
37730-memorials-of-the-independent-churc:
Memorials of the Independent Churches in Northamptonshire is a church history by Thomas Coleman. John Snow published it in London in 1853. Its subtitle adds biographical notices of the pastors. The Puritan ministers who laboured in the county get their own account. The introduction glances at the rise of Nonconformity from the Reformation. Henry the Eighth's break with Rome opens the story.

Many Protestants wanted the reformation carried further than the king allowed. Acts of Uniformity tried to stop all further improvement. Under Elizabeth, returning exiles swelled the dissatisfied ministers' ranks. The Act of 1559 forced a prayer book many could not accept. Those men pleaded for a purer worship and discipline. Hence, Coleman explains, they were called Puritans.
38900-a-chronological-table-of-the-catho:
A Chronological Table of the Catholic Primates of Ireland sets out, see by see, the archbishops of Armagh, Dublin, Cashel, and Tuam. With each name goes the year in which he succeeded to his metropolitan see. The table is a bare work of reference: names in order, a running number for each man, and the year of his succession.

The Armagh list opens the table and shows its scale. St Patrick stands first, succeeding in the year 433. Bineen and Jarlath follow in 465, Cormack in 482, and the line runs unbroken through the early centuries: Ailild the First and Second, Dubtach the First and Second, Feidlimid, Cairlan, and Eochaid. By the year 1000 the list has reached the forty-fourth name. Such a table serves the reader of Irish church history who needs the primates' order and dates at a glance.
39920-yarmouth-notes-1830-1872-collated-:
Yarmouth Notes, 1830 to 1872, collated from the file of the Norwich Mercury by Frederick Danby Palmer, was printed at Great Yarmouth in 1889 by Buckle of King Street. The extracts first ran as a column in the Yarmouth Mercury. Palmer says a general wish from the public brought them into book form. The volume is dedicated to Lord Suffield.

Palmer warns the reader fairly in his preface. The Norwich Mercury was the organ of the old Whig party. Its political notices are tinged by the editor's party feeling, and should be read with that in mind. The idea for the collation came when the Mercury file was given to the Yarmouth Free Library. The notes gather forty years of borough news: elections, storms, trade, and town affairs.
41788-general-gatacre-the-story-of-the-l:
Beatrix Gatacre wrote this life and services of General Gatacre. Murray printed it in London in 1910 with portraits and maps. William Forbes Gatacre lived from 1843 to 1906, the title notes. A Browning line, what I aspired to be, fronts the life.

Contents open with Gatacre youth, then to India and back again. Rangoon, Secunderabad, and the Black Mountain expedition follow in service. Mandalay, Poona, Bombay, Chitral, and Quetta mark his India years. The plague, Atbara and Omdurman, and Cape Colony come late. A Meredith sonnet on worthiness and rivals stands as the life second motto piece.
42457-owen-glyndwr-and-the-last-struggle:
Arthur Granville Bradley wrote this life of Owen Glyndwr for the Heroes of the Nations series, published by Putnam in 1901, with a brief sketch of Welsh history before it. The frontispiece shows Glyndwr's Mount at Glyndyfrdwy.

The introduction sweeps from the Romans in Wales through Cunedda, Howel Dda and his laws, and the Norman conquest of Glamorgan. It ends with Llewelyn the last prince, Edward the First's castles and statutes, and Wales between conquest and the rising. Chapter two gives Owen's birth and early life, 1359 to 1399, his youth, marriage, and seats at Sycherth and Glyndyfrdwy. Chapter three opens the quarrel with Lord Grey of Ruthin and the failed lawsuit. History readers get the last Welsh war of independence.
43691-the-history-of-the-catnach-press-a:
The History of the Catnach Press is a work of printing history by Charles Hindley, published by the author at London in 1886. This is a large paper copy; only 250 were printed, each numbered and signed. Its subject is the two Catnachs, John and James, father and son.

The press worked at Berwick-upon-Tweed, Alnwick, and Newcastle-upon-Tyne in Northumberland. Its fame rests on Seven Dials in London. Jemmy Catnach, the son, was the great ballad printer of that district. Hindley calls him a pioneer of cheap literature. Ballads, penny histories, and street papers poured from the press. Hindley had already written a life of James Catnach and edited the Curiosities of Street Literature. This history gathers the firm's story whole. It preserves a trade that taught the poor to read by giving them print they could afford and wanted.
45676-flower-guide-wild-flowers-east-of-:
Flower Guide: Wild Flowers East of the Rockies is Chester A Reed's pocket guide to identifying the wild flowers of eastern North America. Doubleday, Page and Company of Garden City, New York, issued this revised edition in 1927, with new illustrations. The book's pride is its pictures: three hundred and twenty flowers in color, painted by the author himself.

Reed confines the book chiefly to identification, yet his introduction pauses on the life of a plant. A flower's real work, he notes, is to produce seed, and ripe pollen must reach the sticky stigma for seed to set. Cross-fertilization keeps a species vigorous, as with the higher animals. Reed's bird and flower guides, small, cheap, and accurate, taught a generation of amateurs to name what they found outdoors.
48403-the-kingdom-of-georgia-notes-of-tr:
The Kingdom of Georgia, by Oliver Wardrop, carries the subtitle Notes of Travel in a Land of Women, Wine, and Song. Sampson Low, Marston, Searle, and Rivington published it in London in 1888, with illustrations and maps. Wardrop dedicated the notes, by permission, to Professor James Bryce. He filled out the travel tale with sketches of history, letters, and politics, specimens of the national music, and a bibliography.

The preface opens far from Georgia, at Baalbek, where Wardrop and three companions lie on cushions after dinner. The party, two Frenchmen, an Italian, and an Englishman, solemnly votes censure on Lamartine for painting the ruins too fine. That joke sets the book's tone: a traveller checking famed places against the poets who praised them.
52442-history-of-the-expedition-under-th:
History of the Expedition under the Command of Captains Lewis and Clark, volume two, was printed at Philadelphia by Bradford and Inskeep in 1814. Paul Allen readied the journals for the press. The trip ran in the years 1804, 1805, and 1806, by order of the government of the United States.

The party went to the sources of the Missouri, across the Rocky Mountains, and down the Columbia River to the Pacific Ocean. The rights note was filed on January 22, 1814, in the thirty eighth year of American freedom. Volume one stands as a twin text in the same set. The chapter heads tell of canoes, an Indian sweating bath and burial place, and dangerous rapids. One canoe had a narrow escape. West fans get the first full print of a famed crossing, in its second half.
55824-from-dan-to-beersheba-a-descriptio:
From Dan to Beersheba is a description of Palestine by John P Newman, issued at New York and Cincinnati in a revised edition with copyright in 1892. Newman was a bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church. The subtitle calls Palestine the wonderful land, and the book carries maps and engravings.

The publishers note its adoption into the course of study for Methodist undergraduates. Ministers in training would need the history, topography, and customs of the Holy Land. Newman's prologue adds the latest explorations and discoveries. The first chapter treats the land's two boundaries, its parallel mountains, and its great valley. Sterility and present fertility are weighed together. Flowers, scenery, and the tribes' portions follow, and Palestine is called a world in miniature. The title quotes the old measure of Israel, from its northern town to its southern one.
56062-from-zone-to-zone-or-the-wonderful:
From Zone to Zone ran as number 13 of the Frank Reade Weekly Magazine, issued at New York on January 23, 1903, and sold for 5 cents. Frank Reade Junior, the boy inventor, makes the wonderful trip of the subtitle in his latest air-ship, the Dart. The chapters promise an ice-bound ship, a rescue by airship, a hollow mountain, a storm, a lion hunt, and a fight with huge white bears that swarm over the Dart's deck.

The tale ends at the North Pole, the goal that savants in the story agree no ship or sledge can reach. Frank Tousey published the weekly, and the story is signed only Noname, as the Reade tales usually were. It is dime-novel science adventure at full stretch: invention, polar ice, and wild beasts, all in one trip from zone to zone.
57112-the-loss-of-his-majesty-s-frigate-:
Printed in London in 1808 for sixpence, this pamphlet tells how His Majesty's frigate Anson was wrecked within three miles of Helston, Cornwall, in late December 1807, with about fifty persons lost. The account comes from Captain Lydiard's steward, who stayed close to the captain and whose word the editor asks readers to trust. A second wreck, the Sidney, shares the title page.

The steward's tale begins on December 27, 1807, with the Anson cruising off the Black Rocks as a gale rose. Seas washed away bowsprits and stove in a port, and thick weather hid the land. Twice the ship wore around while the master argued they could make the Lizard and reach Falmouth. The pamphlet adds a full account of the Sidney, lost on a rock on May 20, 1808, with only a few of her crew saved, plus tales of dreadful famines at sea.
58334-the-jewel-house-an-account-of-the-:
The Jewel House is a tale of the royal jewels and the tales of love and crime tied to them, by the keeper of that house himself. He was a major general with a row of high honors to his name. Its front print shows the kings state crown, from a paint made by a named artist.

Bound in with the keepers tale is a lost piece, here set in print for the first time. It is the tale of a famed plot by a bold colonel to steal the crown jewels from the Tower, writ by a man of that age. The book thus weds the lore of crown, orb, and sceptre to true tales of theft, gift, and pomp round the gems of the realm.
58857-the-works-of-william-harvey-m-d-tr:
The Works of William Harvey holds the Latin works of the great doctor in English. Robert Willis turned the texts from Latin and wrote a life of the man. A London society for old medical books put the set out. The book bears the year eighteen forty seven on its title page.

Harvey found how blood runs in a loop through the whole frame. His books on that find and on the birth of beasts form the core here. The front note says most of the chief works stood in English print by then. The editor aim was to give them one sound home in a set. Plates and a full life frame the texts for doctors and scholars.
68794-the-mayflower-society-house-being-:
Walter Merriam Pratt wrote The Mayflower Society House, privately printed at Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1950. Pratt served as Governor-General of the General Society of Mayflower Descendants. His book tells the story of the Edward Winslow House, the Mayflower Society, and the Pilgrims. A second edition, it opens with verses about the dunes and twin lights near Plymouth.

The Society bought the Edward Winslow House in 1941. The house stands on North Street in Plymouth, one of the five streets the Pilgrims laid out. It overlooks Plymouth Rock and Cole's Hill, where many Pilgrims lie buried. North Street was laid out before 1633 and first named New Street. Pratt traces the street's names and owners, from the Howland family to Edward Winslow. The book joins a house history to the story of the society that preserves Pilgrim memory.
9789-army-boys-in-the-french-trenches-or:
Homer Randall wrote Army Boys in the French Trenches in 1919, a boys' war tale of hand-to-hand fighting. The book follows American boys at dawn attacks, between the lines, and in close quarters, with tanks, cavalry, and broken bridges. Colonel Pavet reappears, Nick Rabig acts queerly, and a shadow of treason falls. A familiar voice and a hail of lead test the boys.

Chapters promise a slashing attack, an uplifted knife, and storming the ridge, with rescue from the sky. Randall writes with brisk, patriotic pace. A reader gets a rousing Great War adventure for boys, full of trenches, tanks, and daring deeds.
army-boys-in-the-french-trenches-or-hand: Homer Randall follows American army boys in France as they wait in the trenches, go over the top at dawn, and fight hand to hand. Chapters move from a slashing attack and the uplifted knife to tanks, cavalry, a broken bridge, and rescue from the sky. Frank Sheldon and Bart Raymond anchor the action with loyalty under fire. The book is boys adventure fiction set in the First World War, brisk, plain, and keen on courage.
doe-osti-2574479-enhancing-the-design-of:
A final technical report from Old Dominion University's Sylvain Marsillac and Matt Grau, with co-investigators Matthew Poelker and Joseph Grames at Jefferson Lab and Erdong Wang at Brookhaven, improves spin-polarized photocathodes. These devices supply polarized electron beams for nuclear physics. The targets were ninety percent polarization and quantum efficiency above one percent, a pairing earlier designs struggled to reach together.

Cathodes were grown by metal-organic vapor deposition on gallium arsenide. Two designs were refined: a strained superlattice, and the same stack backed by a distributed Bragg reflector that bounces light back through the active layers. Modeling tuned the reflector's layer pairs, and a doping study tuned the surface layer. Finished devices reached quantum efficiency as high as 2.3 percent with polarization of 92 percent at 780 nanometers. They delivered 11 nanocoulombs of charge in free running, and 9 with an eight-millimeter laser spot.
doe-osti-2589171-reconciling-heliostat-a:
Matthew Emes, Matthew Muller, Matthew Neber, and Guangdong Zhu of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this study, NREL/TP-5000-96375, dated September 2025. It covers wind loads for heliostats, the mirrors that track the sun in concentrating solar power fields. A field holds thousands of mirrors on slender posts. Wind is their main structural enemy.

Solar panels face the same enemy, and their wind load standards are far more mature. The study asks how much of that knowledge transfers. It reviews PV array standards and their geometric similarity to heliostat fields. Then it sets pressure data from wind tunnel experiments and field measurements side by side. Field data come from the Crescent Dunes plant, comparing two edge heliostats with one in the interior. Dynamic loads are worked out by mirror size and wind speed. The goal is a reduced-order model: design-grade loads without a wind tunnel for every field.
doe-osti-2997317-templates-for-risk-info:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-12277R, by Lekha Patel, Garrett Allen, Candace Diaz, and co-authors, dated September 2025, builds templates for risk-informed assurance using the hidden geometry of networks. TRACE, the project name, maps a network into a curved latent space where distance reflects how nodes relate. Odd placements in that map can flag anomalies worth a closer look.

Theory rests on a latent space method credited to Lubold, Chandrasekhar, and McCormick, extended here to mixed-type graphs. Test networks were grown on manifolds with varying curvature to prove the method can recover the true curvature. Construction details set a spacing rule: a chosen radius stays under half the closest vertex gap, and each vertex becomes a small clique of at least three nodes. Security and infrastructure analysts get a geometric lens for spotting structural risk.
doe-osti-2997331-feedforward-control-for:
Sandia National Laboratories slide deck SAND2025-12099R, by Austin Motes, Kenneth Brown, and Josh Paquette, dated 21 July 2025, reports a pilot study on shielding wind turbines from extreme gusts. The idea is feedforward control: sense the wind far upwind, across the whole farm, and yaw and pitch the turbine before the gust arrives. Waiting for the gust to hit leaves no time to unload the blades.

Simulations used standard design load cases, including cases 1.4 and 3.3, with a threshold yaw error triggering action. Two measures clearly improved under combined yaw and pitch feedforward: yaw-bearing moment and blade-root flapwise moment. Limits are stated plainly: the emergency stop was disabled, blade pitch dithering skewed some peak loads high, and real radar processing delays were not modeled. A cost-benefit pass is the named next step.
doe-osti-3399426-commercialization-of-th:
Commercialization of the NLR Hydrogen Wide Area Monitor, HyWAM, is the subject of CRADA final report NLR/TP-5700-99684, dated July 2026, under agreement CRD-18-00784. William Buttner is the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact and cited author. Funding came from the Hydrogen Fuel Cell Technologies Office.

Hydrogen leaks are invisible and odorless, and a fueling station or production hall needs to know about one before gas collects. A wide area monitor watches a whole space rather than a single point, extending the laboratory's hydrogen sensor work into a product form. The cooperative project carried that monitor toward commercialization with an industry partner. The final report closes the agreement and records the work at the level cleared for release.
history-of-the-expedition-under-the-comm:
This first volume gives the official history of the Lewis and Clark expedition. The corps crossed to the sources of the Missouri in 1804 to 1806. It then crossed the Rocky Mountains and ran the Columbia to the Pacific. A map by Samuel Lewis, from Clark's own drawing, fronts the book.

The journal voice is plain and exact, mile by mile. Teapot Island and its neighbors are logged by size and side. Game, weather, rivers, and native peoples fill the daily notes. The captains write as soldiers on a survey, not as romancers. Readers travel the young republic's great western probe in its own words.
podcast-dannyjones-2dY-roDpHWI:
Ammon Hillman studies ancient Greek language and texts, and he brings Danny Jones a thesis built to shock: that early Christian practice involved children and drugs in ways the Church later buried. His reading rests on Greek words he argues translators have softened or misunderstood for centuries.

Hillman works through his textual evidence phrase by phrase, and Jones, to his credit, keeps asking what the words can actually bear. Scholars dispute Hillman's conclusions sharply, and nothing here is settled doctrine or settled history. The episode's value is exposure to a radical philological argument in its author's own words. Listeners should treat it as a claim to be checked against the texts, which is how Hillman himself frames his invitation.
podcast-dannyjones-KXRqcSUUYwI:
Psychologist Sheldon Solomon helped build terror management theory, the idea that awareness of death drives much of human culture. On Danny Jones's podcast, he discusses what he calls the worm at the core of human consciousness: the knowledge that we die, and the civilizations we build to avoid facing it.

Solomon explains the experiments behind the theory, in which reminders of death measurably shift people's politics, faith, and prejudices. Jones tests the idea against the show's usual subjects, cults, conspiracies, and apocalypses, all of which Solomon's framework reads as death-denial in costume. The episode is among the most scholarly in the series, and its claim is unsettling precisely because it is modest and testable. Listeners get a serious thinker's summary of his life's work, in conversation.
podcast-dannyjones-oarGH2UZWWI:
A guest billed as a Venezuelan spy joins Danny Jones to claim a shadow network steers US elections. The episode gives the guest no name in the title. He speaks as a man who worked in that hidden world.

The guest lays out how he says votes, press, and cash are bent from abroad. He names the routes and the fronts he claims do the work. Jones asks what proof a masked claim can bear. Listeners get a spy's dark tale of hidden hands on US votes. The library files the talk as an archive record, and readers judge the tale on its terms.
podcast-joerogan-iIGu2ggjsWI:
Jiu-jitsu legend Rickson Gracie talks about the importance of learning to breathe in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Gracie, unbeaten in his fighting years, treats breath as the base of his famous invisible jiu-jitsu. Rogan, a martial artist himself, listens as a student.

Gracie explains how breath control calms the mind under pressure, in a choke or in daily life. He shares the drills and the philosophy behind them. The segment is a short master class from a man whose calm was a weapon, useful to fighters and yogis alike, and best read slowly.
podcast-tuckercarlson-Su1pWqZFqWI:
Commentator Michael Knowles joins Tucker Carlson to discuss Donald Trump and Israel, the commentator Candace Owens, and Knowles's central claim: that Christianity is booming in America despite the attacks on it. The three topics braid into one argument about faith's political moment, defiant and, in their telling, ascendant.

Knowles, a Catholic conservative with a debater's training, supplies the episode's structure: setback, schism, and revival. Carlson shares the revival thesis; both men cite packed churches and young converts as their evidence. Their reading of the Owens split adds the movement's internal drama. The recording preserves the traditionalist wing of the right explaining itself at a confident moment, useful for any listener tracking how faith and faction now move together.
podcast-tuckercarlson-gMbacDpXoWI:
Tucker Carlson says he has never heard a wrongful prosecution story like Trevor Milton's. Milton founded the Nikola truck firm and was later convicted. Carlson heard the full tale at a dinner the night before.

He calls the case a shocking failure of justice. The title charges that Wall Street and the FBI joined to crush Milton. It claims his tech threatened big oil firms. Milton tells his side step by step. The episode asks viewers who trusted the courts to rethink that trust after hearing his account. The host treats each detail as a fresh shock.
the-camp-fire-girls-do-their-bit-or-over: Hildegard G. Frey wrote The Camp Fire Girls Do Their Bit, or Over the Top with the Winnebagos, put out in New York by the A. L. Burt Company in 1919. The front pages list Frey's Camp Fire set, a series endorsed by the officials of the Camp Fire Girls organization. The first chapter is called A Dream Comes True, and no more of it is shown here.
the-harp-of-god-proof-conclusive-that-mi: J. F. Rutherford wrote The Harp of God, described on its title page as proof conclusive that millions now living will never die. The title page calls the book a text-book for Bible study made for beginners, with many questions and Scripture citations, and it shows a 510,000 edition dated 1921. The publishers named are the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society and the International Bible Students Association of Brooklyn, New York. Only the title page, dedication, and contents heading are present here.
the-history-of-the-great-irish-famine-of: The Rev. John O'Rourke, P.P., M.R.I.A., wrote The History of the Great Irish Famine of 1847, with notices of earlier Irish famines, shown in a third edition printed in Dublin by James Duffy and Co. in 1902. A dedication addresses his fellow countrymen and calls the famine one of the most terrible episodes in the chequered history of their native land. Only the title page and dedication are present here, so the narrative itself does not appear.
